original_claim: Freight fraud dollar losses ($500M-$800M; $40,760/load avg) — all figures trace to TIA 2024 member survey, laundered through trade pubs (single-source chain)
verdict_summary: The $500M-$800M total range can be partially cross-validated by Tier 1 (FBI/IC3) and Tier 3 (Verisk CargoNet, ATRI) sources for directional order of magnitude, though those sources measure all cargo theft rather than freight-fraud-only. The $40,760/load average is confirmed as exclusive to the TIA survey — no independent actuarial, government, or academic source replicates or cross-validates that specific per-load figure. The two sub-claims require different treatment.

new_sources.publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation / Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
new_sources.key_data: FBI PSA Alert I-043026-PSA: 'In 2025, estimated cargo theft losses in the United States and Canada surged to nearly $725 million (60 percent increase from 2024), while confirmed cargo theft incidents increased by 18 percent. The average value per theft rose 36 percent to $273,990, driven by more selective, high-value targets.' Confirms cyber-enabled double-brokering and strategic cargo theft as the dominant and growing method. Cites Verisk CargoNet data as underlying source.
new_sources.supports_claim: Partially. Validates the directional order of magnitude for total losses ($500M-$800M range sits between 2024 measured $455M and 2025 measured $725M). The $725M figure for 2025 exceeds the $800M upper bound only marginally and covers all cargo theft (physical + fraud). Does NOT independently publish a per-load fraud cost figure.
new_sources.notes: This is a primary government source (FBI) that explicitly validates cargo theft loss magnitude. The PSA's dollar figure derives from Verisk CargoNet actuarial data, which is Tier 3, but the FBI endorsement elevates the citation chain to Tier 1 for the total-loss figure.

new_sources.key_data: $454.9M estimated total cargo theft losses in 2024 (3,625 incidents); average value per theft $202,364; fraud/deception incidents (strategic theft) now ~one-third of all incidents by end-2024; strategic theft rose 1,475% between 2022-2024.
new_sources.supports_claim: Partially. Provides the strongest independent cross-validator for total loss magnitude. 2024 measured figure ($455M) is below the $500M lower bound but consistent with the order of magnitude. The fraud-only subset would be a fraction of this total, meaning $40,760/load and $500M-$800M cannot both be simultaneously accurate unless total fraud loads numbered ~12,000-20,000 annually — not validated.

new_sources.key_data: $725M estimated total cargo theft losses in 2025 (60% increase from 2024's $455M); average loss per theft $273,990 in 2025.
new_sources.supports_claim: Supports the upper end of the $500M-$800M range for 2025. But this covers all cargo theft types, not fraud-only.

new_sources.publisher: American Transportation Research Institute (ATRI) — non-profit affiliated with American Trucking Associations
new_sources.key_data: ATRI 'The Fight Against Cargo Theft' (October 2025): Surveyed 95 for-hire carriers + logistics service providers (LSPs). LSPs (freight brokers, 3PLs) average $1.84M in annual theft losses; motor carriers average $520K/year. Industry-wide extrapolated cost: $1.8B-$6.6B (direct + indirect). Notably for LSPs, 62.5% of theft incidents were strategic/fraud-type. Survey-implied LSP per-incident average ~$100K (vs TIA's $40,760/load). ATRI explicitly notes severe underreporting bias.
new_sources.supports_claim: Partially. Independently confirms large-scale financial impact on freight brokers from fraud-type theft (strategic). However, ATRI's LSP-specific per-incident figure (~$100K) is 2.5x higher than TIA's $40,760/load, suggesting the TIA figure may undercount per-load costs or measure a different subset. Neither figure is directly comparable without methodology alignment.

new_sources.publisher: TT Club (marine and logistics insurer) + BSI Consulting
new_sources.key_data: Strategic theft now accounts for ~18% of all US cargo theft incidents in 2024. US-specific: electronics lead stolen products (19% of thefts); 79% of US thefts involve trucks. No per-incident US dollar figure published in this report. Globally, online fraud is cited as a US$500bn industry.
new_sources.supports_claim: Corroborates the scale and prevalence of strategic fraud in US freight. Does not independently quantify per-load or total-industry dollar losses for freight fraud specifically. No cross-validation of $40,760/load or $500M-$800M range possible from this source.

total_loss_range_500M_800M.finding: The $500M-$800M range is directionally supportable but requires careful framing. Verisk CargoNet measured $455M in 2024 (all theft types, US+Canada) and $725M in 2025. The FBI/IC3 (Tier 1) independently confirmed the $725M 2025 figure. If the original claim refers to fraud-only losses (not all cargo theft), the $500M-$800M range significantly overstates what actuarial sources independently measure for that subset. TIA's own estimate was revised upward from $500M-$700M to 'in excess of $1B' by January 2025, indicating the lower bound is stale. The $800M upper bound appears unattributed in any primary source — TIA cited $700M in 2023, and its president cited $800M+ verbally without a published source.
total_loss_range_500M_800M.recommended_treatment: Replace single-source TIA citation with: Verisk CargoNet measured $455M in 2024 and $725M in 2025 for all US+Canada cargo theft (physical + fraud combined), independently confirmed by FBI/IC3 (April 2026 PSA). TIA's member-survey estimate of $500M-$1B+ for freight-payment fraud represents a broader definition that includes payment fraud not captured in CargoNet's incident-tracking.

per_load_average_40760.finding: The $40,760/load figure is exclusively derived from the TIA 2024 member survey of ~200 industry professionals (Feb-Aug 2024). No government (FBI, FMCSA, DOT), actuarial (CargoNet, NICB), or independent academic source publishes a per-load freight fraud cost figure. The calculation methodology is: $402,344 average annual loss per company divided by an unstated number of loads — the denominator is not disclosed in TIA's published report. ATRI's LSP-specific data (October 2025) implies a per-incident average of ~$100K for fraud-type thefts, which is 2.5x the TIA figure. Verisk CargoNet's overall average per theft ($202,364 in 2024, $273,990 in 2025) is 5-7x higher than $40,760, but those are for all theft types including high-value physical cargo theft. There is no independent source that validates $40,760 as the cost of a single fraudulent load event.
per_load_average_40760.recommended_treatment: Mark as [ASSUMED-N] or drop from canonical claims. The figure cannot be independently validated and its methodology is opaque. If retained, must be explicitly labeled as 'TIA member survey of ~200 respondents, methodology not publicly disclosed.'

source_genealogy_note: The $40,760/load figure provenance: TIA Fraud Report (Feb-Aug 2024, n~200 member survey) → FreightCaviar article → TruckingDive → Freightwaves → downstream uses in Stage 2. Every downstream citation resolves to the same TIA PDF. The $500M-$800M range: lower bound ($500M-$700M) from TIA (undisclosed methodology circa 2022-2023); upper bound ($800M+) verbally attributed to TIA president with no published source. Neither figure has an independent actuarial, government, or academic primary source. The closest independent validators (Verisk CargoNet, ATRI, FBI/IC3) measure related but not identical phenomena at different loss magnitudes.
suggested_revision: Split the claim into two separately-supported assertions: (1) 'Total US+Canada cargo theft losses (physical + fraud combined) reached $455M in 2024 and $725M in 2025, per Verisk CargoNet actuarial tracking independently confirmed by FBI/IC3 (April 2026 PSA).' Tier 1-3. (2) 'Industry-association surveys (TIA, n~200 freight brokers, 2024) estimate per-company fraud losses at ~$402K/year and imply a per-load cost of ~$40,760, though this figure has no independent actuarial cross-validation and the calculation methodology is not publicly disclosed.' Tier 6, survey-derived.
suggested_new_score: Medium (for total-loss magnitude, now cross-validated by Tier 1-3 sources) / Low-confirmed-scarce (for $40,760/load specific figure)
reasoning: Two distinct sub-claims require different verdicts. The total-loss order of magnitude ($500M-$800M range) is now cross-validated by FBI/IC3 Tier 1 and Verisk CargoNet Tier 3 sources, though those sources cover all cargo theft (not fraud-only) and bracket the range rather than confirming it exactly. The $40,760/load figure remains exclusively TIA-sourced with no independent validator found after exhaustive search across all six priority source categories; it should be marked as assumed/unvalidated in the canonical draft.
